title: Canada Child Benefit
subtitle: Turn a tax return you almost skipped into a monthly deposit that reaches your kitchen table

blocks.text: A monthly deposit from the government sounds like the setup to a scam call. This one is real, it's yours if you qualify, and the only trick is filing your taxes on time.

The Canada Child Benefit pays families who qualify a tax-free amount every month for each child under 18. See how the CRA sets your payment, meet the two income limits that shrink it, and learn the paperwork mistake that pauses even a family that qualifies. The goal is a file you can defend, not a guess you hope survives contact with the CRA.
The CCB is not added to your income and does not need to be reported as income on your tax return. It is calculated from your return, but it is not part of it.

items.title: “The CCB counts as income, so I'll owe tax on it.”
items.text: It's tax-free. It never gets added to your income, and you never pay it back at tax time just for receiving it.

blocks.text: CRA: Canada child benefit overview
Two income numbers decide whether your family gets the full payment or a shrunken one.
blocks.detail: Crossing the higher threshold without knowing it is what turns an ordinary reduction into a confusing surprise on deposit day.
blocks.extra: The four things that set your number come next.

sections.title: How the CRA Calculates Your Payment

blocks.text: Four things move the number on your deposit. None of them require a calculator you don't already own.

items.title: HOUSEHOLD INCOME
items.text: Your adjusted family net income (AFNI) combines your net income with your spouse or partner's. More income above the threshold shrinks the payment. It does not erase it.

items.title: AGES OF YOUR KIDS
items.text: Each child under 6 is worth more than a child aged 6 to 17. A birthday or a new baby changes your total mid-year, automatically.

items.title: YOUR TAX RETURN
items.text: CRA recalculates every July using the return you filed that spring. A late or missing return can pause your payment completely, no matter your income.

items.title: CUSTODY ARRANGEMENT
items.text: Full-time, primary, or shared custody changes who applies and how the amount gets divided between two homes.

blocks.text: For the July 2026–June 2027 benefit year, the maximum is $8,157 a year ($679.75 a month) for a child under 6, and $6,883 a year ($573.58 a month) for a child aged 6 to 17. These figures are indexed every July. Check canada.ca for the current numbers.

Below $38,237 in AFNI, you get the full amount with no reduction. Between $38,237 and $82,847, the reduction percentage climbs with each child, from 7% for one child to 23% for four or more. Above $82,847, a fixed amount plus a smaller percentage applies to the extra income.

items.title: “Earning any amount over the threshold cuts off the whole benefit.”
items.text: Income above the threshold shrinks the payment gradually. It almost never drops straight to zero unless household income is high.

blocks.text: CRA: How we calculate your CCB
Meet Marcus
paragraphs: Marcus Ferreira drives a delivery van in Hamilton. His daughter Mia stays with him four nights out of every seven. That is real, close to equal parenting, not “visits.” His goal this October is small: buy Mia winter boots without a crack across the toe. Her old pair lets in slush like it was built for wading.

Marcus and Mia’s mother, Priya, split up a year and a half ago. Priya always handled “the government stuff.” When a coworker brings up the Canada Child Benefit, Marcus laughs. “That goes to moms,” he says. “Everybody knows that.”

His coworker shares custody of his own son, and he says that is not true. Marcus looks it up on his lunch break. The CRA page says the benefit goes to whoever mainly cares for the child. If two parents split time close to equally, each one can apply for half.

He almost closes the laptop. He did not file a tax return last year. He was between jobs for three months and earned almost nothing, so a return with nothing on it felt pointless. The page says something he does not want to hear: no return, no benefit, income or not.

He could let it go. The boots would wait, and taxes feel like a fight. Instead, he decides to file. It takes forty minutes and one annoyed call to his sister for an old T4 slip. He fills out the CRA’s shared custody form and checks his account two days later. It says his payment is zero.

His first thought is that the whole thing is a government-shaped joke. His second thought, the useful one, is to call and ask why. The agent tells him his address on file is three moves out of date. That sent his claim to a slow manual review.

He fixes the address. Nine days later, a payment lands. It is half of what Mia is worth on paper, backdated for the months the file was stuck. He spends the first deposit on the boots. Purple, a bit ridiculous, fully waterproof. Mia wears them through every puddle on the walk to school, which is the universal sign of a satisfied customer.

blocks.text: Marcus's file was correct. It was his address that was wrong. Address mismatches are the most common reason a shared-custody claim stalls in review.
What actually fixed it?
A five-minute address correction, not a stronger application. He also learned the return had to exist before the benefit could.
Marcus's shared-custody claim was correct. His address on file was three moves out of date.
blocks.detail: One outdated field on a CRA account paused a payment he'd already earned, and a five-minute fix brought it back.
blocks.extra: The four boxes that prove you qualify are next.

blocks.text: Four boxes, and most families tick all of them without realizing it.

items.title: LIVE WITH THE CHILD
items.text: You live with the child, and they're under 18.

items.title: PRIMARY CARE
items.text: You’re mainly responsible for their day-to-day care: meals, school, appointments, the whole job.

items.title: STATUS IN CANADA
items.text: You or your spouse or partner is a citizen, permanent resident, protected person, or a temporary resident who's lived here 18 months or more.

items.title: TAXES FILED, EVERY YEAR
items.text: You and your spouse or partner file a return annually, even in a year with zero income.

blocks.text: Shared custody is defined as the child living with you at least 40% of the time, or on an approximately equal basis between two addresses. Both caregivers apply, and both must report any custody change to the CRA right away.

New parents can apply through the Automated Benefits Application when they register a birth, instead of filing separate paperwork later. A child approved for the disability tax credit can also add the Child Disability Benefit on top of the regular payment, and most provinces fold their own child benefit into the same monthly deposit.

items.title: “Only mothers can get the Canada Child Benefit.”
items.text: Whoever mainly handles the child’s day-to-day care can apply, of any gender and any relationship to the child. Parents who share custody can each get half.

items.title: “You need to be a Canadian citizen to receive it.”
items.text: Permanent residents, protected persons, and even some temporary residents who've lived in Canada 18 months or more can qualify. Citizenship isn't required.

sections.title: Quick Check: Choose the Best Next Move

items.title: Your family's AFNI is $30,000, with two kids ages 4 and 9. What happens to your payment?
items.detail: Nothing shrinks. Full maximum for both kids. Your AFNI sits below the $38,237 no-reduction threshold.

items.title: Your child turns 6 partway through the benefit year. What changes?
items.detail: The payment steps down to the 6-to-17 rate starting the month after the birthday. The CRA adjusts it on its own, with no form needed.

items.title: You and your ex split time with your daughter close to equally, but only your ex has ever applied. What should you do?
items.detail: Apply as a shared-custody caregiver through CRA My Account or form RC66. Once approved, you start getting your half going forward.

items.title: You forgot to file last year's taxes. Does that cancel this year's CCB?
items.detail: It pauses it. File your return, and your spouse or partner's if you have one, and CRA recalculates, often with a retroactive payment once it's processed.

items.title: Your one-child family's AFNI jumps from $70,000 to $95,000 this year. What happens next July?
items.detail: Next July's payment drops, using the second-threshold formula on the higher income. This July's payment stays put. It's still based on last year's lower AFNI.

sections.title: Your Action (Fill Out Form): Your Benefit File

blocks.text: Short answers, plain language. This is preparation, not tax or legal advice.
A complete file doesn't guarantee a payment amount. It makes a delayed or incorrect one much faster to catch and fix.

items.title: Canada Child Benefit (CCB)
items.text: A tax-free monthly payment from the Canada Revenue Agency that helps eligible families cover the cost of raising a child under 18.

items.title: Adjusted family net income (AFNI)
items.text: The income number the CRA uses to set your payment. It is your net income plus your spouse or common-law partner’s, with a few deductions applied.

items.title: Benefit year
items.text: The 12-month stretch from July to June where your CCB amount stays fixed, based on the tax return you filed the spring before.

items.title: Shared custody
items.text: An arrangement where a child splits time close to equally between two homes that aren't the same household. Each caregiver can get half of what they'd receive with full-time custody.

items.title: Automated Benefits Application
items.text: A one-step option that lets new parents apply for the CCB while registering their baby's birth, instead of filing a separate form later.

items.title: Child Disability Benefit
items.text: An extra tax-free monthly amount added on top of the CCB for a child approved for the disability tax credit.
